summary: Specifies a shared LISP message type for defining future extensions and running experiments without using up a LISP Packet Type codepoint for each one. It also creates an IANA registry for these extensions. It obsoletes RFC 8113. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Instead of making a new mailbox slot for every new idea, this makes one shared slot with sub-labels, so experiments do not use up the limited slots.

questions: what is the lisp shared extension message
how to define new lisp message types
subtitle: A shared message slot for LISP extensions to avoid exhausting limited codepoints.

tldr.problem: LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) defines message types using 4-bit codepoints, limiting the space to 16 possible messages. With multiple extensions proposed, this space fills up quickly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9304 reserves one LISP message type (type 15) as a shared extension message. Each extension uses that message type with a sub-type identifier to distinguish itself. Sub-types are registered in a new IANA registry.
tldr.outcome: LISP extensions can be defined without exhausting the limited type space, and experiments can be deployed with less bureaucracy. RFC 9304 also promotes RFC 8113 from Experimental to Standards Track.

today: RFC 9304 is a standards-track specification that obsoletes RFC 8113. It establishes the shared extension message type as the mechanism for extending LISP without consuming the limited type codepoint space.

sections.title: The LISP Extensibility Problem
sections.content:
LISP is a routing protocol that separates an identifier (who you are) from a locator (where you are) to enable more flexible network architecture. LISP messages have a type field that can hold values 0 through 15 (a 4-bit space), allowing only 16 different message types.

RFC 9304 addresses the limited type space by defining a shared extension message type (type 15). Instead of assigning a new codepoint to each extension, all extensions use type 15 with different sub-types. This allows dozens of extensions without exhausting the base type space.
sections.eli5: LISP has only 16 mailbox slots. Rather than use one for each new idea, all new ideas share one slot and use sub-labels inside it.

sections.title: How the Shared Message Works
sections.content:
The shared extension message has a fixed header: a type field set to 15, followed by a sub-type field that identifies the specific extension. The remaining bytes are extension-specific.

Sub-types in the range 0 through 1,023 are assigned via Standards Action, reserved for protocols with broad consensus. Sub-types 1,024 through 4,095 are assigned on a First Come, First Served basis, allowing faster deployment of experiments.
sections.eli5: The shared message says Type: 15, Sub-type: X where X tells you which extension it is.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
RFC 9304 creates a new IANA registry called LISP Shared Extension Message Type Sub-types. It also updates the existing LISP Packet Types registry to point to RFC 9304 instead of RFC 8113.

The sub-type registry reserves the 0-1023 range for standards-track specifications and the 1024-4095 range for experimental and less formal allocations. This balance between controlled and rapid allocation supports both stability and innovation.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps track of which sub-types are assigned and who uses them.
